blocks.text: ENT examination is extremely common in pediatric OSCEs. You may be asked to examine the **ear, nose, throat, oral cavity, tonsils, neck or cervical lymph nodes**, or perform a complete ENT examination.
A good pediatric ENT examination is:
**“Examine the ears of this child and present your findings.”**
**“Perform an ENT examination on this child.”**
**“Examine this child with recurrent ear infections.”**
**“Examine this child with suspected enlarged adenoids.”**
Approach the child at their level.
“Hello, my name is Dr ____. I have been asked to examine your ears, nose and throat today.”
“Could I confirm your child's name and age?”
“I'm going to have a look inside your ears, nose and mouth. It shouldn't hurt, although the ear examination may feel a little unusual.”
Don't immediately put the otoscope into the child's ear.
You can let the child see or hold the otoscope if appropriate.
Before examining the ENT system, observe the child.
Pain with tragal pressure can occur in:
This is one of the most important pediatric ENT OSCE skills.
“I'm going to gently look inside your ear. Try to keep your head still.”
For a young child, the parent may help stabilize them.
Hold the otoscope like a pen.
Use your little finger against the child's cheek/head to provide stability.
This means if the child suddenly moves, your hand moves with them rather than pushing the speculum deeper.
**Never insert the otoscope deeply or forcefully.**
This helps straighten the external auditory canal.

blocks.title: A normal tympanic membrane should be:

items.text: With a visible cone of light

blocks.text: **“The right tympanic membrane is erythematous, opaque and bulging, with loss of the normal landmarks and cone of light. These findings are consistent with acute otitis media.”**
**“The left tympanic membrane appears dull and retracted with an amber-colored middle-ear effusion and reduced mobility. These findings are suggestive of otitis media with effusion.”**
You may see an obvious hole.

**“There is a central perforation of the right tympanic membrane with associated middle-ear discharge. The findings are consistent with a perforated tympanic membrane, likely in the setting of otitis media.”**
Don't automatically call every perforation chronic suppurative otitis media; correlate with history and discharge.

blocks.title: A retracted tympanic membrane may appear:

blocks.text: “The tympanic membrane is retracted with prominent middle-ear landmarks, suggestive of negative middle-ear pressure from Eustachian tube dysfunction.”
**“There is a retraction pocket in the attic containing keratinous debris, with associated abnormal tympanic membrane appearance. This raises concern for cholesteatoma.”**
**“The external auditory canal is erythematous, swollen and contains debris. The child has significant pain on movement of the tragus and pinna. These findings are consistent with otitis externa.”**
“There is a significant amount of cerumen partially obstructing the left external auditory canal, limiting visualization of the tympanic membrane.”
“The tympanic membrane cannot be visualized because of impacted cerumen.”
“There is a foreign body visible within the external auditory canal. The tympanic membrane cannot be adequately assessed beyond the obstruction.”
**“There is erythema, swelling and tenderness over the right mastoid with outward displacement of the pinna. These findings are concerning for mastoiditis.”**
Ask the child to breathe through the nose if cooperative.
“There is a unilateral foul-smelling purulent discharge from the right nostril, raising suspicion of a retained nasal foreign body.”
**“The nasal mucosa is pale and boggy with enlarged inferior turbinates and clear rhinorrhea, consistent with allergic rhinitis.”**
Adenoids cannot normally be directly visualized with a simple anterior nasal examination.
“The child has persistent mouth breathing, a hyponasal voice and features suggestive of chronic nasal obstruction. In the clinical context, adenoidal hypertrophy would be an important consideration.”
Ask the child to open their mouth.
Use a tongue depressor only when necessary.
“There is poor dental hygiene with multiple carious teeth, particularly involving the upper and lower molars.”
Ask the child to protrude the tongue.
**Hypoglossal nerve dysfunction**, depending on the clinical context.

White plaques over the tongue, palate or buccal mucosa.

**“There are several small, mobile, mildly tender anterior cervical lymph nodes, the largest approximately 1 cm, with no overlying skin changes. This is consistent with reactive cervical lymphadenopathy.”**
**“There is a firm, non-tender, relatively fixed cervical lymph node measuring approximately 3 cm, with no overlying skin changes. This is concerning and would require further evaluation.”**
Do not immediately say "malignancy" unless the clinical context supports it.
If multiple nodal groups are enlarged:
“There is generalized lymphadenopathy involving the cervical and axillary regions, with nodes that are predominantly mobile and non-tender. This would warrant a broader systemic assessment.”

blocks.title: Hearing assessment is particularly important in:

blocks.text: Whisper numbers/words and ask them to repeat.
For very young children, formal audiological testing may be needed.
A child who does not respond to your voice does **not automatically have hearing loss**.
“I would complete my assessment by checking the child's temperature and vital signs and performing a full systemic examination if clinically indicated.”
“I would also arrange formal hearing assessment if there were concerns about hearing.”
“I would also assess the frequency and severity of previous episodes and ask about obstructive sleep symptoms.”

**“This is a well-appearing child with no respiratory distress. There is no facial asymmetry, nasal obstruction or abnormal voice. The external ears are normal bilaterally with no discharge or mastoid tenderness. Both external auditory canals are patent and the tympanic membranes are intact, pearly grey and with normal landmarks. The nasal mucosa is healthy with no significant discharge or obstruction. The oral cavity is clean with no ulcers or lesions. The tonsils are not enlarged and there is no exudate. The posterior pharynx is normal. There is no significant cervical lymphadenopathy. Overall, this is an unremarkable ENT examination.”**
This is the section I'll expand significantly going forward.

**“The child appears mildly unwell. The right tympanic membrane is bulging, erythematous and opaque, with loss of the normal landmarks and cone of light. The left ear is normal. These findings are consistent with acute right otitis media.”**

**“The right tympanic membrane is dull and retracted with an amber appearance and visible air bubbles behind the membrane. There is no obvious acute inflammation. These findings suggest a right middle-ear effusion.”**

**“The right external auditory canal is markedly erythematous and edematous with debris and discharge. There is significant pain on manipulation of the tragus and pinna. The findings are consistent with acute otitis externa.”**
**“There is a visible central perforation of the left tympanic membrane with purulent middle-ear discharge. The findings are suggestive of a perforated otitis media.”**
**“There is marked post-auricular erythema, swelling and tenderness with anterior displacement of the pinna. These findings are concerning for mastoiditis and require urgent assessment.”**
**“The child has pale, boggy nasal mucosa with enlarged inferior turbinates and clear rhinorrhea. There is no purulent discharge. These findings are consistent with allergic rhinitis.”**
**“There is unilateral foul-smelling purulent discharge from the right nostril, with visible material within the nasal passage. This is highly suggestive of a retained nasal foreign body.”**
**“The child has persistent mouth breathing, a hyponasal voice and symptoms of chronic nasal obstruction. The clinical picture is suggestive of significant adenoidal hypertrophy.”**
**“The tonsils are bilaterally enlarged and erythematous with patchy white exudates. There are tender anterior cervical lymph nodes. These findings are consistent with acute tonsillitis.”**

**“There is unilateral enlargement of the left tonsil and peritonsillar region with deviation of the uvula to the right. The child has a muffled voice and difficulty opening the mouth. These findings are highly concerning for a left peritonsillar abscess.”**
**“There are multiple adherent white plaques involving the tongue and buccal mucosa, with underlying erythema. The appearance is consistent with oral candidiasis.”**

**“There are multiple small, mobile and mildly tender anterior cervical lymph nodes, with no fixation or overlying skin changes. In this clinical context, the findings are most consistent with reactive lymphadenopathy.”**
**“There is a 3-centimetre firm, non-tender and relatively fixed cervical lymph node. There are no overlying inflammatory skin changes. This is abnormal and requires further investigation.”**

**“There is cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy involving multiple nodal groups. The nodes are predominantly mobile and non-tender. This represents generalized lymphadenopathy and warrants systemic evaluation.”**

**“The child demonstrates reduced response to whispered sounds in the left ear compared with the right. Rinne testing suggests a conductive deficit on the left, and Weber lateralizes to the left. These findings are consistent with left-sided conductive hearing loss.”**

content_groups.group_title: Q: What are the landmarks of the normal tympanic membrane?

blocks.text: Handle of malleus, lateral process of malleus, umbo and cone of light.

content_groups.group_title: Q: How do you differentiate otitis externa from otitis media?

blocks.text: Otitis externa primarily affects the external auditory canal and typically causes pain with movement of the tragus or pinna. Otitis media involves the middle ear and produces characteristic tympanic membrane abnormalities.

blocks.text: **Otitis media with effusion is a very important/common cause.**

blocks.text: **Large, hard, fixed, progressively enlarging, supraclavicular, persistent, generalized, or associated with systemic symptoms.**
❌ Using an inappropriate or excessively large speculum.
❌ Forgetting to stabilize your hand against the child's head.
❌ Pulling the pinna in the wrong direction for the child's age.
❌ Saying "red eardrum = otitis media" without assessing the tympanic membrane as a whole.
❌ Looking only at the tonsils and forgetting the rest of the mouth.
❌ Calling every enlarged cervical node malignant.
❌ Performing an aggressive throat examination in a child with possible airway compromise.
